messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Amir was forty years old, a paramedic for over fifteen years, married with two children, and he had always thought of himself as someone who kept his head when others lost theirs. That ended on a Tuesday evening in late October, during a call that began as a routine response to a reported stabbing in a convenience store parking lot. His partner, Elena, was two years younger than him, quick-witted and steady, and they had worked together long enough to read each other’s movements without words. When they arrived, the scene was chaotic—a young man bleeding from a femoral wound, a woman screaming, bystanders filming on their phones. Amir knelt to apply pressure while Elena radioed for backup and began directing traffic. He did not see the second assailant emerge from behind the dumpster. He only heard the sound—a wet, hard crack—and then Elena was on the ground, her skull fractured by a steel pipe. He stayed with her, tried to stop the bleeding from her ear, but she was gone before the helicopter landed. In the weeks that followed, Amir could not stop replaying that moment: the sound, the way her eyes went blank, the warmth of her blood on his gloves. But there were gaps too—whole seconds he could not account for, like the time between hearing the crack and finding himself kneeling beside her. He had tried to fill them in, but the effort only made the memories that did come back feel more vivid, more real, until remembering her face brought the same cold terror he had felt in that parking lot.

At first, Amir went back to work the next week. It seemed like the right thing to do—the only thing he knew how to do. But soon the work itself became a trap. Every visible injury, every wound he dressed or tourniquet he applied, was Elena’s wound. Every victim he tried to calm was her. The antiseptic smell of the hospital emergency bay—sharp and chemical—hit him like a physical blow, flooding his sinuses with the memory of the helicopter’s interior and the futile resuscitation. He began to dread his shifts, but he could not bring himself to call in sick. Instead, he worked longer hours, took extra shifts, volunteered for the busiest stations. He told himself he was being dedicated, but the real reason was simpler: as long as he was running from call to call, he did not have time to think. The moment he stopped—sitting in the crew room, driving home in silence—the thoughts would rush in, and he would force them back down, clenching his jaw until his temples ached. He had come to believe that if he let himself remember fully, he would never be able to function again. So he suppressed, and he worked, and he suppressed again.

But the avoidance bled into everything. He stopped attending the monthly training sessions at the firehouse because the classroom smelled like the hospital. He started sitting with his back to the wall in every room—at the station, at home, even in his own living room. If his wife touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he would flinch so hard he sometimes knocked her hand away. Concentration became a daily struggle: he would lose track of conversations mid-sentence, forget to eat lunch, drive past his exit on the way home. His wife noticed he was distant, irritable, and often wakeful; she assumed it was grief, and it was, but it was also something more tangled. Amir felt he had permanently changed for the worse, that the man who used to joke with his crew and sleep through the night was gone. Worse, he had begun to believe that he could not rely on himself any longer. If he had been more alert, if he had scanned the parking lot better, he could have seen the second man. He should have protected Elena. She was his partner, his responsibility, and he had failed. The thought sat in his chest like a stone, and no amount of overtime could dislodge it.

What finally brought him to seek help was a shift three weeks ago. He was assigned to a call for an elderly man who had fallen and gashed his forehead. The wound was minor, but when Amir leaned in to clean it, the sight of the torn skin, the hospital antiseptic smell from the man’s own bathroom, and the memory of Elena’s head all fused into one seamless, horrifying moment. He could not move. He stood frozen, his heart hammering, the room dissolving around him until a colleague touched his arm and he yelped, stumbling backward. After that, his supervisor gently suggested he take time off. At home, alone with the silence, Amir finally admitted he could not keep going this way. He is afraid of what therapy might uncover—afraid that fully remembering will destroy him, or that he will discover he was never the man he thought he was. But he is also hoping, quietly, that there might be a way to live without the terror, without the constant watchfulness, without feeling that he has already failed everyone who matters.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Avoid Work or Study: The vignette does not show the patient avoiding going to work or study; instead, he overworks by taking extra shifts and working longer hours.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Amir was forty years old, a paramedic for over fifteen years, married with two children, and he had always thought of himself as someone who kept his head when others lost theirs. That ended on a Tuesday evening in late October, during a call that began as a routine response to a reported stabbing in a convenience store parking lot. His partner, Elena, was two years younger than him, quick-witted and steady, and they had worked together long enough to read each other’s movements without words. When they arrived, the scene was chaotic—a young man bleeding from a femoral wound, a woman screaming, bystanders filming on their phones. Amir knelt to apply pressure while Elena radioed for backup and began directing traffic. He did not see the second assailant emerge from behind the dumpster. He only heard the sound—a wet, hard crack—and then Elena was on the ground, her skull fractured by a steel pipe. He stayed with her, tried to stop the bleeding from her ear, but she was gone before the helicopter landed. In the weeks that followed, Amir could not stop replaying that moment: the sound, the way her eyes went blank, the warmth of her blood on his gloves. But there were gaps too—whole seconds he could not account for, like the time between hearing the crack and finding himself kneeling beside her. He had tried to fill them in, but the effort only made the memories that did come back feel more vivid, more real, until remembering her face brought the same cold terror he had felt in that parking lot.

At first, Amir went back to work the next week. It seemed like the right thing to do—the only thing he knew how to do. But soon the work itself became a trap. Every visible injury, every wound he dressed or tourniquet he applied, was Elena’s wound. Every victim he tried to calm was her. The antiseptic smell of the hospital emergency bay—sharp and chemical—hit him like a physical blow, flooding his sinuses with the memory of the helicopter’s interior and the futile resuscitation. He began to dread his shifts, and within two weeks he started calling in sick. He would wake up on a Monday morning and feel his stomach clench, his heart race, and he would pick up his phone and leave a voicemail for dispatch—short, apologetic, a lie about a fever. The first time felt like failure; the tenth time felt like relief. He stopped answering calls from his supervisor. He stopped looking at the schedule when it was posted. He told himself he just needed a few days to clear his head, but the days turned into weeks. The station became a place he could not bear to imagine, let alone enter. He had come to believe that if he let himself go back, he would either break down in front of his crew or freeze on a call and let someone else die.

But the avoidance bled into everything. He stopped attending the monthly training sessions at the firehouse because the classroom smelled like the hospital. He started sitting with his back to the wall in every room—at home, in his own living room, even when he went to the grocery store. If his wife touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he would flinch so hard he sometimes knocked her hand away. Concentration became a daily struggle: he would lose track of conversations mid-sentence, forget to eat lunch, drive past his exit on the way home. His wife noticed he was distant, irritable, and often wakeful; she assumed it was grief, and it was, but it was also something more tangled. Amir felt he had permanently changed for the worse, that the man who used to joke with his crew and sleep through the night was gone. Worse, he had begun to believe that he could not rely on himself any longer. If he had been more alert, if he had scanned the parking lot better, he could have seen the second man. He should have protected Elena. She was his partner, his responsibility, and he had failed. The thought sat in his chest like a stone, and no amount of staying home could dislodge it.

What finally brought him to seek help was a shift three weeks ago—the only one he had forced himself to take in over a month, partly out of guilt and partly because his supervisor had gently suggested he might be ready to try. He was assigned to a call for an elderly man who had fallen and gashed his forehead. The wound was minor, but when Amir leaned in to clean it, the sight of the torn skin, the hospital antiseptic smell from the man’s own bathroom, and the memory of Elena’s head all fused into one seamless, horrifying moment. He could not move. He stood frozen, his heart hammering, the room dissolving around him until a colleague touched his arm and he yelped, stumbling backward. After that, his supervisor called him in and told him to take medical leave. At home, alone with the silence, Amir finally admitted he could not keep going this way. He is afraid of what therapy might uncover—afraid that fully remembering will destroy him, or that he will discover he was never the man he thought he was. But he is also hoping, quietly, that there might be a way to live without the terror, without the constant watchfulness, without the crushing weight of having failed Elena, and without the shame of being a paramedic who can no longer go to work.
